_comment: Which Pythons this project is held to, in one place, because three different files
used to answer that question and nothing checked that they agreed.
Three things are deliberately separate here, and conflating them is the mistake this
file exists to prevent:
A. `minimum` and `blocking` are SOURCE compatibility. They say which interpreters
the code in src/, tests/ and scripts/ must run on. Widening them is a promise
about the source, and nothing else.
B. `bundled_runtime` is what a release actually ships inside the archive, so an
ordinary user needs no Python at all. It is pinned on purpose and moves only
when somebody decides to move it. Adding a version to `blocking` must never
change it: a release's bytes are not allowed to drift because CI grew a lane.
C. A user's own system Python is not a supported input to anything. It matters
only to a contributor running the engine from a source checkout.
`minimum` stays where it is unless there is a separate, explicit decision. This is a
packaged Windows application, not a library whose value depends on running on old
system interpreters, so there is nothing to gain by reaching downward for a bigger
version count - and every version added is one more that has to keep passing.
`blocking` ends with the newest released line (3.15 since 2026-10-31, the owner: the CI for source
runs must run the newest Python; only the newest line is required). That lane asks setup-python for
the newest release of its line (`check-latest`), and no other lane does.
`future_prerelease` is the next Python while it is still a release candidate, or null while there is
none to run - it is null now. When the next Python reaches beta, set it here and add its experimental
lane to .github/workflows/test.yml (ten `include` entries and `allow-prereleases`; 10 more jobs, so the
36-37 jobs a run may take must be made room for first). That lane runs for real - it compiles the
sources and runs the same suite - and annotates its failures like any other, but it does not block a
merge, because a defect in a pre-release interpreter is not a defect in this product. When it ships,
move it into `blocking` and set the next one here (or null); `tests/test_python_support.py` fails if the
workflow and this file stop agreeing, in either direction.
Reproducibility note, which is why the release line is named: on Windows, Python 3.14
and later use zlib-ng, and it compresses the same files to different bytes. A digest
comparison has to use `release_build` - CONTRIBUTING.md and docs/VERIFY.md say so.
